analysis.one_liner: Doubles the price large, wealthy investors pay to buy single-family homes, funding affordable housing.
analysis.headline: The bill to tax large investors 100% on single-family home purchases never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would charge wealthy investors a tax equal to the full price of any single-family home or small duplex they buy — effectively doubling the cost, making such purchases unattractive. It would not apply to a wealthy individual's own primary residence or to purchases made under government low-income housing programs. Money raised would go into the federal Housing Trust Fund for affordable housing, and HUD would publish yearly reports on investor home-buying trends.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and first-time homebuyers would face less competition for houses on the market, because a tax equal to the full purchase price would make it uneconomical for wealthy investors to buy homes and rent them out [S2][S3]. Revenue from the tax would go to the federal Housing Trust Fund, which funds affordable housing [S3].

how_it_helps.text: By making it uneconomical for investors to buy single-family homes, the bill would leave more houses available for families to buy or rent, easing pressure on prices driven up by investor demand
All tax revenue collected would be transferred to the Housing Trust Fund, which funds construction and preservation of affordable housing
The bill would require HUD to publish an annual public report on investor purchases of single-family homes, giving policymakers and the public a factual record of investor activity

analysis.who_pays: Large investors — companies and individuals whose assets exceed $20 million — would pay a tax equal to 100% of the purchase price of any single-family home or duplex they buy, unless it becomes their own residence or part of a government low-income housing program [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors with over $20 million in assets

drawbacks.text: The $20 million asset threshold is based on a person's or entity's total assets, not on how many homes they own, so it reaches wealthy individuals buying second homes and small landlords, not only large institutional investors — anyone with over $20 million in assets buying an investment property would pay the tax

The bill only covers single-family homes and duplexes (one to two dwelling units), so investors could shift to buying townhouses in bulk, small apartment buildings, or land to build rentals, avoiding the tax entirely

Blocking investor purchases does not itself build new housing; in some markets investors convert homes to rentals, and critics of such measures argue that restricting them could reduce the available rental supply even as it helps prospective homebuyers

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core goal — taking deep-pocketed investors out of the single-family home market — would directly help ordinary buyers and renters, and the revenue would fund affordable housing. But the design has real weaknesses: the $20 million asset test catches wealthy individuals buying investment properties generally rather than targeting big institutional buyers specifically, and the one-to-two-unit limit leaves investors an easy path through apartment buildings, condos, and land purchases. It would also have needed enforcement of the controlled-group rules across corporate webs to be effective. The idea is pointed at a real problem, but the version introduced is a blunt instrument with gaps.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees in July 2022 and neither one ever took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 28, 2022, late in the two-year session, and was referred to two committees: Ways and Means (which handles taxes) and Financial Services (which handles housing)
Neither committee took any action — no hearings, no markup, no vote — and the bill received no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023
It had the support of 8 Democratic cosponsors and no recorded Republican support, and no companion bill in the Senate appears in the provided record

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large investors — including institutional landlords and wealthy individuals — remain free to buy single-family homes without any added tax, continuing to compete with ordinary buyers. No revenue was generated for affordable housing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large investors who buy single-family homes

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental landlords and home-flipping investors
industries.note: A 100% excise tax would make buying single-family homes and duplexes economically impossible for investors with over $20 million in assets, ending a major source of their rental revenue. Because the bill died, their business model is unchanged.

industries.industry: Wealthy individual landlords (households with over $20 million in assets)
industries.note: The tax would fall on individuals with more than $20 million in assets who buy single-family homes as rental or investment properties, though their own principal residence is exempt.

industries.industry: Residential real estate brokerages and mortgage lenders
industries.note: The tax would reduce the pool of buyers for single-family homes, cutting investor-driven sales volume. It also takes some deep-pocketed bidders out of the market, which could benefit ordinary homebuyers.
